To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the performance of aged rats is impaired in the water maze task, (b) this impairment is evident in the first trial of each of the second, fourth and fifth days of training, (c) this impairment is not evident in the last trial of any of the days of training, and (d) these findings indicate that the aged rats do not learn to solve the spatial task.

(1) the 24-month-day animals take significantly longer to find a platform submerged in water (spatial task) than do the 6-month animals, (2) the performance of 24-month-old rats in the spatial task is similar to that of 12-month-day rats,

age-related impairments of spatial memory were evident in the first trial of each of the first four days of testing and that age-related impairment of spatial memory were not evident in the last trial of any of the first four testing days.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of age-related cognitive deficits.
the effects of aging on spatial memory.
age-related impairments of spatial memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 24-month animals performed more poorly than the 6-month animals in the spatial condition; the 12-month animals fell between the other two groups.

the 12-month animals performed similarly to the 24-month animals in the first trial of each of the second, the third, and the fourth days of testing, but performed similarly to the six-month animals in the last trial of these three days.

the age-related deficits in the performance of the rats in the water maze were not a consequence of a general decline in the ability to swim and to learn, but were specific for the task and were related to the age-related changes in the ability to acquire and store spatial memory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

age-related impairments of learning and memory are temporally graded, with the earliest deficits occurring in the acquisition of new information and the latest deficits occurring in the retrieval of previously learned information.
age-related deficits in spatial memory are not uniform over time and that there are two components to this deficit.
the performance of the aged rats was indistinguishable on the first trial from the young adult and aged animals, but was indistinguishable by the end of the day.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 6-, 24-month-old rats were indistinguishable from each other when tested on the last trial in the water maze on the fifth day of testing.
age-related cognitive impairments are not static.
age-related cognitive impairments in the Morris watermaze can be detected as early as 12 months, but only in the context of a temporal sampling strategy.
